title: The Weight of Still Water
author: E. H. Sarrow
description: Six long chapters, each of them the better part of an hour's reading. An archivist is sent to catalogue the village of Hallowmere in the six months before a reservoir drowns it, and finds a parish register that records five deaths and a churchyard that holds three. A quiet novel about paperwork, which is to say about what a community agrees to write down. blocks.c: One: The Commission
The valley was to be flooded in October, and Ilse Vanterpool was given until then to write down what was in it.

She drove up on the first Monday in April with the county's grey estate car full of boxes, and stopped where the new road stopped, at a gate with a Water Board sign on it, and got out to open the gate herself because there was nobody else within four miles to do it. The morning smelled of wet stone. Below her the Ashlie went down its own valley in the way rivers do when they have never been argued with, in long slow bends across a flat green floor, past a church tower, past a mill, past thirty-one roofs of grey slate, and out of sight around the shoulder of the hill where the men from the Board had built their dam.

The dam was finished. That was the thing she had not been ready for. In her head the commission had a quality of the hypothetical — a valley that was going to be flooded, one day, by a dam that was going to be built — and here it was already, a wall of pale concrete across the neck of the valley with a crane on top of it and a temporary bridge and four sheds, and behind it, on the far side, nothing yet but a wet meadow and a river that did not know.
She stood at the gate for some minutes and looked at it.

Then she got back in the car and drove down into Hallowmere, and the road went under a beech avenue and came out at a green, and she parked outside a public house with its windows boarded and its sign taken down, and that was the beginning of it.
The scope of the work
The letter of commission ran to two pages and had been written by a man who had clearly been told to make it sound larger than it was.

The Contractor shall prepare a full inventory and photographic record of the fabric, contents and monuments of the parish of Hallowmere prior to inundation, together with such documentary material as may be recovered from the parish chest, the school, and other public buildings, and shall deposit the same with the County Record Office. The Contractor's attention is drawn to the Board's programme, under which the valley floor must be cleared by 30 September.

Ilse had read it four times on the train down to the interview and had recognised it for what it was: a line item. Somewhere in the estimate for a dam that had cost eleven million pounds there was a figure of two thousand, four hundred pounds against the words historical record, and she was that figure, and the figure existed because a member of the county council had asked a question in the spring of the year the scheme went through, and because it is cheaper to employ an archivist for six months than to be asked the question again.

She did not mind. She had spent fourteen years in a basement in the county town listing other people's papers and had long ago made her peace with being a line item; a line item is a thing that gets done.
What she minded, in the first week, was the size of it.

They had told her there were thirty-one houses. There were thirty-one houses, and a church, and a chapel, and a school, and a mill with a wheel in it, and a smithy that had not been a smithy since before the war and was full of the smith's grandson's furniture, and a village hall with a stage and a piano and forty-one folding chairs, and a shop, and a bus shelter, and a war memorial, and eleven barns, and two hundred and six gravestones, and a Victorian pumping engine in a shed at the bottom of the lane which nobody had mentioned to her at any point and which turned out to be the only working example of its type in the country.

She wrote to the Record Office at the end of the first week and asked for an assistant. They wrote back and said that there was no provision for an assistant, and enclosed, as though it were a comfort, a copy of the estimate showing the figure of two thousand, four hundred pounds.
Mr. Cordell

The Board's resident engineer was called Hollis Cordell and he came to find her on the Thursday, in the church, where she was on her knees with a tape measure and a torch trying to establish whether a stone in the chancel floor was a slab or a ledger.
"Miss Vanterpool? Cordell. I'm told I have to be nice to you."
"Told by whom?"

"By the Board's solicitor, who says you have a statutory right to be here, and by my wife, who says you're doing the only decent part of this whole job." He was a heavy, tired man of about fifty in a good coat and terrible boots. "I've brought you the keys to the school and the hall, and a list of the properties we've already stripped, and I would like to say one thing before you decide what you think of me."
"Go on."

"I have flooded two valleys. This is my third. In the first one, in the fifties, the Board took the view that a village which is going to be under ninety feet of water does not need to be recorded, and they cleared it in eleven weeks, and there is now not one photograph of the inside of any building in that place, and I have thought about it every year since." He put the keys on the pew. "So take what you want. Take the doors off if you want. If anybody from my office tells you that you cannot go into a building, send them to me."
Ilse got up off her knees.
"Thank you," she said. "May I ask what the programme actually is? I have been told October."

"The gates close on the first of October, weather allowing. After that the water comes up at about a foot a week for the first month, faster after, and the floor of the valley is under by Christmas and the church tower goes under in the spring." He said it without any particular emotion, the way a man says a timetable he has said many times. "There are three things that must happen before the gates close, Miss Vanterpool, and I want you to know all three now rather than in August."
"Please."

"One. Every building on the valley floor must be demolished to below the level of the future water. That is not vandalism, whatever they write in the newspapers; a floating roof timber is a hazard to a dam. Two. The graves must be moved." He looked at the floor of the chancel. "All of them. Two hundred and six stones and whatever is under them, to the new ground at Culverton. That is a licence job and it starts in July."
"And three?"
"Three," said Cordell, "is Mr. Pike."
The village, before

It is worth setting down what Hallowmere was, because in six months it was not going to be anything, and because the whole of what follows depends on it having been a real place with a real number of people in it.

Two hundred and forty souls in 1940. Thirty-one houses on the valley floor and eleven more up the sides, of which nine were farms. A church, a chapel, a school, a mill, a shop with a post office counter in it, a public house called the Ashlie Arms, a village hall built by subscription in 1922 as a war memorial and used four nights a week ever since.
By the year the scheme went through there were sixty-one people. By the spring Ilse came there was one.

That is not the dam's fault, or not entirely. The county's own figures showed the population halving between 1931 and 1961, before anybody had drawn a line on a map, for the reasons every upland parish in the country halved: the milk price, the buses, the pull of the towns, and the simple fact that a young man who has seen somewhere else will generally go there. The dam did not kill Hallowmere. The dam arrived at the bedside.

Ilse thought about this a great deal in her first fortnight and eventually wrote a paragraph about it in her interim report, which the Board's solicitor asked her to remove on the grounds that it was editorial. She removed it from the report and kept it in the file, with a note recording that it had been removed and by whom, which is what you do.
Mr. Pike

Every drowned valley has one and Hallowmere's was Emrys Pike, sixty-five years old, of Ford Cottage, the last inhabitant, who had refused the Board's offer four times and had refused the Board's improved offer twice and had told the Board's land agent, in writing, that he would be at home.

He kept bees. That was the first thing Ilse learned about him, from Cordell, and it turned out to be the most useful thing anybody ever told her, because Emrys Pike would not discuss the valley or the dam or the compensation or the law, but he would discuss bees at any hour of the day or night with any person who asked, and he could not stop himself, and this was the crack in him through which everything else eventually came.
She went to Ford Cottage on the Friday of the first week with a notebook and no plan.

It was the last house on the lane, past the mill, with the river on one side and eleven hives on the other in a row facing south-east, and the door was open, and a man was sitting at a table under the window writing in a ledger with a fountain pen.
"You'll be the record woman," he said, without looking up.
"Ilse Vanterpool."
"I know. Cordell told me. You've been in the church all week measuring the floor." He finished a line and blotted it. "You'll want to record my house."
"If you'll let me. Not today."

That got her a look. He had a long face, badly shaved, and very pale eyes, and something about the way he sat — squared to the table, both forearms on it — reminded her powerfully of somebody and she could not think who.
"Why not today?"

"Because today I want to ask you about the bees," said Ilse, "and I have been told that if I ask you about the bees I will not get away before dark, and I have four hours of daylight and a church to finish."
Emrys Pike put down his pen.
"Sit down," he said. "You'll have tea. It's got to be tea, I've no coffee, and the milk's tinned."
She was there until nine.
What the bees were for

He kept eleven stocks and had kept bees since he was thirteen. He told her the whole management of them in the order a beekeeper thinks of things, which is not the order anybody else would use: the spring build-up first, then swarming, then the summer flow off the lime trees on the drive at Ashe House, then the heather in August up on the top, which is what the valley bees were famous for, then the winter feed and the mouse guards and the long anxious months of not knowing.
At about seven o'clock, over the third pot of tea, Ilse asked the question she had been holding since four.
"Mr. Pike. What happens to them in October?"
The room went quiet in a way rooms do.
"They'll go up to Culverton," he said. "There's a field. It's arranged."
"And you?"
"I'll go where the bees go."
"I was told you'd refused four offers."

"I have refused four offers," said Emrys Pike, "and I will refuse the next four, and when the water is over the doorstep I will get into the van with the hives and I will drive to Culverton, and everybody will say, well, he came round in the end, and everybody will be wrong." He turned the ledger on the table so that it faced her: a beekeeper's record, hive by hive, year by year, in a hand that had not changed in thirty years. "You're an archivist. You'll understand this and Cordell won't. It isn't the house. It isn't the land. It's that when I go up to Culverton I stop being from here, and being from here is the only thing about me that has ever been true."
Ilse looked at the ledger.
Hive 1. Hive 2. Swarm taken from the ash, 12 May. Requeened 3 June, dark queen, own stock. Fed 14 lb, 20 September.
Forty years of a man writing down small facts because they were his.
"That," she said, "is more or less the definition of my profession, Mr. Pike."
"Aye. Well." He shut the ledger. "That's why I've let you sit here for five hours."
The parish chest

The church of St. Ivo at Hallowmere is a small building of no particular architectural distinction, with a fifteenth-century tower, a nave rebuilt in 1837 after a fire, and a chancel which is the oldest part and which has a stone floor of ledger slabs, of which Ilse eventually catalogued nineteen.

On the wall of the nave, above the door, there is a painted board of the eighteenth century recording a bequest, and Ilse copied it out on her second morning because painted boards are always the first thing to go when a building is stripped and nobody ever thinks to record them:

GIVEN BY MR. JOHN AYNSCOMBE OF THIS PARISH
ANNO 1741
The rent of four acres called Long Meadow
for bread to be laid on this table
every Sunday for ever
and for the teaching of four poor children
of Hallowmere to read.

Long Meadow is under the reservoir. There has been no bread on that table since 1913, when the charity was consolidated by the Commissioners into a fund that now pays for a book prize at a comprehensive school eleven miles away, and Ilse traced the whole chain of it in September and put a note of it in the finding aid, and that note is the only reason anybody now knows why the prize is called the Aynscombe.

The parish chest was in the vestry: an iron-bound oak box of the seventeenth century, four feet long, with three locks and one key, which meant that the other two had been forced at some point in the past and nobody had ever mentioned it.
She opened it on the Monday of the second week, alone, in the cold, with a torch in her teeth, and this is what was in it, and she listed it that evening in her working notebook exactly as follows:

items: Register of baptisms, marriages and burials, 1561-1699. Vellum, limp binding, water damage to first eleven leaves.
Register of baptisms, 1700-1812; register of marriages 1754-1812; register of burials 1700-1812. Three volumes, calf.
Registers of baptisms, marriages and burials, printed forms, 1813 to date. Eleven volumes.
Overseers of the poor, accounts and settlement examinations, 1698-1834. Bundle, string-tied, damp.
Plan of the churchyard, showing numbered plots, on linen, undated, annotated in three hands.
Sundry: two bundles of unsorted correspondence, a box of parish magazines, a tin of collection counting slips, an unopened bottle of communion wine, and a mousetrap.

blocks.c: It was, she wrote in her notebook that night, a good chest. She meant it as a professional judgement and it was the highest praise she had.

She began work on the registers on the Tuesday and it took her the rest of April, and it was in that fortnight, without noticing that she had noticed it, that she first went past the thing that afterwards took over her life.
February 1942
The burial register in use during the war is the eleventh of the printed-form volumes, and it covers 1924 to 1961, and it is unremarkable in every way except one.

Between the twelfth and the twenty-second of February 1942, in a village of two hundred and forty souls, the rector recorded five burials, all of them children, all of them between the ages of six and twelve.
No. 411. Rhys, Marta. Age 11. Abode: Hallowmere. Buried 14 February 1942. By me, T. J. Ammons, Rector.
No. 412. Pike, Emrys. Age 12. Abode: Hallowmere. Buried 14 February 1942. By me, T. J. Ammons, Rector.
No. 413. Callow, Grace. Age 6. Abode: Hallowmere. Buried 17 February 1942. By me, T. J. Ammons, Rector.
No. 414. Braith, Nell. Age 10. Abode: Ferrisport, evacuated. Buried 21 February 1942. By me, T. J. Ammons, Rector.
No. 415. Braith, Tomas. Age 12. Abode: Ferrisport, evacuated. Buried 21 February 1942. By me, T. J. Ammons, Rector.
Five children in nine days.

Ilse read it, and copied it, and made a note in the margin of her working sheet — diphtheria? check newspapers, MOH reports — and went on to the next page, because she had four hundred and eleven entries to transcribe and six months to do everything in, and because a rural parish losing five children to an epidemic in the winter of 1942 is a sad thing but not a strange one.
It sat in her, though.

It sat in her for eleven days, in the way a wrong note sits in a piece of music you are not listening to closely, and it came up out of her on the last Friday in April, in the church, at four in the afternoon, when she had finished the registers and had begun on the plan of the churchyard.

The plan is on linen, about three feet by two, and shows the churchyard divided into numbered plots, and it has been annotated by at least three different people over what she later established was a period of about ninety years. It is not a complete record. Nobody ever kept a complete record. But it is good, and it is careful, and where a burial is known the plot carries a number that keys to the burial register.
She found 413, Grace Callow, in the south-east corner, under the yew, with her plot number in a hand of the 1940s.
She found 411 and 412, Marta Rhys and Emrys Pike, side by side in the same corner, in the same hand.
She looked for 414 and 415 for two hours, and they were not there.

She went out into the churchyard with the plan and a torch as the light went, and she walked the south-east corner in the wet grass, and she found the yew, and she found Grace Callow's small stone, and beside it two smaller stones with no names on them at all, only initials and a date, M.R. and E.P., 1942.
Three graves.
And in the register, five children.
Ilse

She went back to the caravan the Board had lent her, which stood on the hard-standing behind the village hall and which she had come to be fond of, and she made her supper, and she sat with the transcription in front of her and did not eat it.
It is worth saying, here, what sort of person she was, because everything that follows turns on it.

Ilse Vanterpool was thirty-nine. She had been an archivist for fourteen years and an assistant archivist for four before that. She was unmarried and had been engaged once, briefly, at twenty-six, to a man who had wanted her to be less exacting, and she had ended it herself, and had never seriously regretted it, and had noticed that she had never seriously regretted it, and had wondered what that said about her.

She was good at her work in a specific way: she was not a historian, and did not want to be. Historians want to know what happened. Ilse wanted to know what was written down, and by whom, and when, and what had been done to the paper since. She had a professional distrust of narrative and a professional love of discrepancy. She believed, in the plain way that other people believe in a religion, that a record honestly kept is the only defence an ordinary person has against being rewritten by whoever comes after them.
And her mother had died the previous winter, in a nursing home in the county town, of a slow illness, at the age of sixty-two.
Her mother's name had been Marta.

Ilse had known that for thirty-nine years and had not thought about it at all, at the moment she copied out entry number 411, because Marta is a common enough name in that part of the country and because a woman who dies in a nursing home at sixty-two cannot have been buried at eleven years old in a valley she never once mentioned.

It came to her that evening in the caravan, with the paraffin heater ticking, and it came in the sideways manner such things do: not as a thought but as a small physical sensation, a lifting, as though the floor had gone briefly soft.
She wrote it down at once, because that is what she was.

25 April. Note. Burial register 1924-61 records five child burials 12-22 Feb 1942. Churchyard plan and stones account for three (Callow 6, and two marked only M.R. and E.P.). The two Braith children (evacuees, Ferrisport) are not on the plan and have no stone. Possible: separate plot, unrecorded; possible: bodies returned to Ferrisport for burial, in which case the entry should not be in this register at all.
Note also, for my own sake and with no evidential value whatever: my mother was born in 1931, was evacuated from a city in 1940 with her school, would not speak about it, and was called Marta.
She looked at what she had written for a while.
Then she added one more line, in the way she had been taught, when a record raises a question that the record cannot answer:
Query. Not resolved. To be revisited.

She did not sleep much. At about two she got up and made tea and stood in the door of the caravan in her coat, looking down the valley at the one light burning in it, which was a beekeeper's window a quarter of a mile away, where a man of sixty-five who could not leave was sitting up with the ledger he had kept for forty years.
She thought: that is a man whose name is on a gravestone under the yew.
Emrys Pike, aged twelve, buried the fourteenth of February 1942.
And in the morning she went down and asked him about swarm control, and did not ask him about anything else at all, for another five weeks.
